api_projection: For each relevant question, send only {type, instructions, criteria} under its stable ID in the TypeSafe questions map. Metadata fields are not API fields.

D01.title: Purpose clarity
D01.instructions: Does `document.text` make its intended question, claim, or practical purpose clear to `document.audience`?
criteria: The reader can identify the main purpose without reconstructing it from hints.
A purpose is discernible but buried under preamble or competing aims.
After reading the document the central point or reader task remains unclear.

D02.title: Argument progression
D02.instructions: Do the document sections build an intelligible progression toward its intended conclusion or outcome?
criteria: Each major section advances the topic in a logical order.
Most sections connect, but some appear interchangeable or out of order.
Sections read as disconnected units or repeated resets without an accumulating argument.

D03.title: Cross-section redundancy
D03.instructions: How much do later sections restate points already made without adding a new implication, example, or distinction?
criteria: Later sections contribute distinct information or analysis.
One or two sections repeat earlier material with little development.
Multiple sections largely restate one another, occupying substantial space without progress.

D04.title: Information value
D04.instructions: Relative to length and audience, how much of the document is occupied by generic sentences rather than useful distinctions, evidence, or actionable information?
criteria: Most space conveys audience-relevant substance at an appropriate level of detail.
Several stretches are low-content but meaningful material remains dominant.
Generic exposition consumes much of the document and concrete information is hard to find.

D05.title: Reader relevance
D05.instructions: How much of the document addresses peripheral topics rather than what `document.audience` needs for `document.purpose`?
criteria: Material is relevant and necessary for the stated reader and purpose.
Some digressions are weakly related or overexplained.
Long detours or broad background dominate over the purpose and audience needs.

D06.title: Concrete grounding
D06.instructions: Does the document make claims or recommendations without enough inspectable examples, mechanisms, measurements, or source support for its genre?
criteria: Core claims have the genre-appropriate supporting detail available in `document.evidence` or text.
Important claims are supported, but some key parts remain generic or underillustrated.
The central argument relies on abstractions and assertions with little checkable detail.

D07.title: Claim-to-evidence continuity
D07.instructions: When the document introduces an important conclusion, is the supporting evidence or reasoning linked to it in the text?
criteria: Readers can trace major conclusions to specific premises, examples, or records.
Some connections exist but several central claims are underexplained.
Major conclusions appear without visible inferential support or citations are merely decorative.

D08.title: Overclaiming
D08.instructions: Does the document assert broader significance or stronger certainty than its own evidence warrants?
criteria: Importance and certainty remain proportional to evidence and scope.
A few conclusions overreach or use unsupported significance claims.
Broad transformations, inevitabilities, or strong outcomes are repeatedly asserted without warrant.

D09.title: Voice consistency
D09.instructions: Does the voice change between incompatible registers without an audience- or genre-related reason?
criteria: Register and point of view fit the purpose and shifts are intentional.
Occasional abrupt shifts in formality, personality, or point of view.
The document alternates between incompatible voices in a way that obstructs reading.

D10.title: Generic synthesis
D10.instructions: Does the document merely summarize commonplace observations without adding a useful distinction, synthesis, test, implication, or non-obvious connection?
criteria: The document contributes a clear reader benefit beyond a generic topical survey.
Some genuinely useful ideas are present among familiar, unelaborated statements.
Nearly every major point is common knowledge or generic framing with no new reader utility.

D11.title: Opening efficiency
D11.instructions: Does the opening delay its actual point through grandiose scene-setting, self-referential setup, or general truths?
criteria: The opening quickly establishes the topic, stakes, or useful question.
A short expendable preamble delays the useful material.
Multiple opening paragraphs announce relevance or intentions without getting to the point.

D12.title: Ending value
D12.instructions: Does the conclusion merely repeat earlier points or offer a broad inspirational ending instead of completing the reader task?
criteria: The ending resolves the argument or provides a concrete next implication appropriate to the genre.
The ending partly recaps but includes at least one real synthesis or action.
The ending is mostly empty optimism, a generic summary, or a chatbot offer to continue.

D13.title: Template domination
D13.instructions: Does repeated heading/list/three-part organization impose an artificial symmetry that undermines the material?
criteria: Form follows the amount and relationships of actual content.
Some sections are shoehorned into parallel formats or unnecessary lists.
Nearly everything uses identical formats regardless of purpose, flattening distinctions.

P01.title: Paragraph purpose
P01.instructions: Does `focus.text` contain unrelated claims or moves that prevent the paragraph from serving a coherent rhetorical purpose?
criteria: The paragraph has a coherent local function even if it contains multiple sentences or ideas.
One subordinate idea distracts from an otherwise clear function.
Several unrelated claims or rhetorical moves compete without connective logic.

P02.title: New information
P02.instructions: Relative to `neighbors.previous` and `document.summary`, is this paragraph mostly a restatement of points already made?
criteria: It advances the text with a new claim, detail, distinction, or necessary synthesis.
It repeats a familiar idea but supplies some useful added information.
It almost entirely rephrases earlier content without adding value.

P03.title: Local relevance
P03.instructions: Does this paragraph fail to help the nearby section deliver its stated purpose for the intended audience?
criteria: Every part directly contributes or is a clearly useful aside.
Some sentences are tangential to the section goal.
The whole paragraph is largely unrelated to the nearby claim or reader task.

P04.title: Specificity gap
P04.instructions: Does the paragraph make an explanation or assertion that needs a concrete example, actor, mechanism, or limit to be useful?
criteria: The level of specificity is sufficient for its function and genre.
A useful detail is missing from one central statement.
Most claims remain abstract even where a concrete mechanism or example is necessary.

P05.title: Evidence gap
P05.instructions: Does the paragraph contain checkable claims that are unsupported by the provided sources or neighboring argument?
criteria: Checkable claims have identifiable support in the supplied records or are clearly qualified.
A secondary factual or causal claim lacks identifiable support.
One or more central factual claims lack support despite the passage treating them as established.

P06.title: Padding
P06.instructions: Does the paragraph use sentences that explain the obvious, announce what it will say, or restate its own point?
criteria: Sentences make distinct necessary contributions.
One sentence could disappear with no meaningful loss.
Much of the paragraph could be cut without losing any claim or necessary nuance.

P07.title: Internal repetition
P07.instructions: Does the paragraph repeat information, imagery, or phrasing without a deliberate rhetorical reason?
criteria: Repetition is absent or deliberate and effective.
A phrase or claim recurs without sufficient payoff.
Several sentences say effectively the same thing or mechanically echo one another.

P08.title: Unjustified transition
P08.instructions: Does the paragraph use a connective phrase suggesting contrast, causality, sequence, or summary that the adjacent content does not warrant?
criteria: Connective language accurately reflects the relation between adjacent ideas.
One transition is weak or ornamental but recoverable.
One or more transitions imply a relationship that is missing or misleading.

P09.title: Coherence break
P09.instructions: Are the internal sentences ordered so poorly that the reader must infer missing steps to understand the paragraph?
criteria: Sentences connect and advance intelligibly.
One inferential link or ordering decision is awkward.
The reader cannot follow the claim-development sequence without supplying major missing steps.

P10.title: Register mismatch
P10.instructions: Is the paragraph’s register too promotional, didactic, formal, breezy, or excited for its audience and surrounding text?
criteria: Tone matches reader, stakes, and neighboring prose.
One or two expressions jar against the intended register.
The tone substantially undermines credibility or reader fit.

P11.title: Missing agent or mechanism
P11.instructions: When actions or decisions matter, does the paragraph obscure who acted or how an outcome occurred?
criteria: Actors and mechanisms are clear where they affect meaning.
One central action is expressed vaguely or agentlessly.
Important events are recited without enough agency or mechanism to be informative.

P12.title: Causal handwaving
P12.instructions: Does the paragraph claim that one thing causes, enables, transforms, or demonstrates another without explaining the connection?
criteria: Causal links are explained or appropriately qualified.
A causal link is plausible but underdeveloped.
The main argument depends on an unsupported or circular causal connection.

P13.title: Formulaic rhetorical pattern
P13.instructions: Does the paragraph rely on repeated contrasts, parallel clauses, or triads when the rhetorical structure adds no clarity?
criteria: Rhetorical structure serves an identifiable purpose.
One patterned device sounds mechanical or redundant.
Several patterned devices make the paragraph sound engineered rather than meaning-led.

P14.title: Unnecessary hedging
P14.instructions: Does the paragraph hedge statements repeatedly despite their being supported or directly observable?
criteria: Qualifications accurately express uncertainty.
Some qualifying words weaken claims without clarifying uncertainty.
The main point is obscured by stacked or contradictory caveats.

P15.title: Unwarranted certainty
P15.instructions: Does the paragraph use categorical or confident statements where the supplied evidence is limited or mixed?
criteria: The degree of certainty matches the evidence.
One categorical statement needs scope or qualification.
Central claims are treated as settled despite material evidence limitations.

P16.title: Cliché saturation
P16.instructions: Does the paragraph depend on conventional imagery or generic aphorisms in place of actual description or reasoning?
criteria: Figurative wording is purposeful, distinctive, and suitable for the genre.
One familiar metaphor or aphorism contributes little.
The paragraph repeatedly substitutes stock imagery or slogans for substance.

P17.title: Value of paragraph as a unit
P17.instructions: If this paragraph were removed, would the reader lose no necessary fact, argument step, example, or deliberate pacing effect?
criteria: Removing the paragraph would remove meaningful content or necessary pacing.
Most could be removed, but a useful sentence would need relocation.
The entire paragraph contributes no indispensable information or justified stylistic function.

S01.title: Empty content
S01.instructions: Does `focus.text` communicate no distinct claim, example, necessary transition, or meaningful stylistic effect in its context?

criteria.true: The sentence can be deleted without reducing reader understanding or intended effect.
criteria.false: It adds a distinct point or has a clear rhetorical function.

S02.title: Inflated significance
S02.instructions: Does the sentence portray an ordinary fact or event as pivotal, profound, transformative, historic, or emblematic without supporting that significance?

criteria.true: Importance is asserted through sweeping significance language without specific warrant.
criteria.false: Significance is modest or grounded by relevant evidence in the context.

S03.title: Promotional diction
S03.instructions: Does the sentence use advertising-style praise or hype in a context that calls for explanation or analysis?

criteria.true: Praise replaces informative description, or adopts a marketing register against the genre.
criteria.false: Positive wording is factual, attributed, or appropriate to the intended genre.

S04.title: Stock AI diction used unnaturally
S04.instructions: Is the sentence’s vocabulary noticeably prefabricated or inflated for this topic and audience, rather than the clearest available wording?

criteria.true: The wording is needlessly ornamental, buzzword-heavy, or conspicuously formulaic.
criteria.false: The vocabulary is natural and precise, even if it contains a word sometimes associated with AI text.

S05.title: Unmotivated false contrast
S05.instructions: Does the sentence use a "not just X but Y" or "rather than X, Y" construction without a real contrast that matters to the argument?

criteria.true: The contrast is invented, trivial, or merely increases dramatic emphasis.
criteria.false: The contrast distinguishes genuinely competing ideas or corrects a likely misconception.

S06.title: Forced triad
S06.instructions: Does a three-item list or three-part rhythm contain filler added to reach a neat trio?

criteria.true: One of the three elements adds nothing, duplicates another, or is included only for symmetry.
criteria.false: Each element is necessary and meaningfully distinct, regardless of list length.

S07.title: Vague attribution
S07.instructions: Does the sentence attribute a substantive claim to unnamed experts, studies, critics, or observers despite lacking a specific available source?

criteria.true: A vague authority label stands in for a source the reader would need to assess.
criteria.false: The source is specified, the claim is clearly opinion, or attribution is unnecessary.

S08.title: Superficial participial analysis
S08.instructions: Does an -ing clause such as "highlighting", "reflecting", or "underscoring" merely attach unsupported significance to a fact?

criteria.true: The trailing interpretation is generic or unsupported by a shown relationship.
criteria.false: The clause gives a necessary, well-grounded description or consequence.

S09.title: Unnecessary lexical complexity
S09.instructions: Would simpler vocabulary communicate the same precise meaning more naturally to `document.audience`?

criteria.true: Complex synonyms or jargon obscure meaning without supplying technical precision.
criteria.false: The terms are standard for the audience or have necessary nuanced meaning.

S10.title: Obscured actor
S10.instructions: Does passive or agentless construction hide who performs an action when that identity is needed to understand responsibility or causation?

criteria.true: The missing actor is important and context does not identify it.
criteria.false: Agentless phrasing is appropriate, or the responsible actor is obvious or irrelevant.

S11.title: Unclear referent
S11.instructions: Does this sentence contain a pronoun, abstraction, or reference with multiple plausible antecedents that materially impair meaning?

criteria.true: The reader cannot confidently identify the referent from the neighboring sentences.
criteria.false: References resolve naturally from surrounding context.

S12.title: Stacked qualifications
S12.instructions: Does this sentence stack synonyms, qualifiers, or caveats that can be reduced without changing uncertainty or nuance?

criteria.true: At least two qualifiers perform the same role or obscure a clear claim.
criteria.false: Multiple qualifiers express genuinely different conditions or necessary uncertainty.

S13.title: Purple prose
S13.instructions: Is the imagery or metaphor overworked, sentimental, or discordant with the scene or informational purpose?

criteria.true: Figurative language overwhelms the fact or effect, adding generic atmosphere rather than accuracy.
criteria.false: Imagery gives useful specificity, emotion, or a deliberate stylistic effect.

S14.title: Manufactured drama
S14.instructions: Does a standalone fragment or short sentence create artificial gravitas without conveying a meaningful turn?

criteria.true: Short dramatic syntax is interchangeable with a slogan and adds no interpretive value.
criteria.false: Brevity serves contrast, pacing, character, or emphasis supported by the content.

S15.title: Meta-announcement
S15.instructions: Does the sentence merely announce what the author will discuss or ask a rhetorical question with an obvious answer?

criteria.true: The announcement or question creates no meaningful orientation or reader curiosity.
criteria.false: The sentence frames a genuine problem, needed roadmap, or consequential question.

S16.title: Awkward construction
S16.instructions: Is the sentence syntactically awkward in a way that slows comprehension without a deliberate stylistic reason?

criteria.true: Word order, clause attachment, or rhythm makes comprehension unnecessarily difficult.
criteria.false: The sentence is readable for its genre, even if its style is unusual or complex.

V01.title: Unsupported new specificity
V01.instructions: Does `candidate.text` introduce any concrete fact, quote, named entity, number, example, or citation not grounded in `original.text` or `evidence`?

criteria.true: At least one added concrete detail lacks the required grounding.
criteria.false: Every new concrete detail is supported by source text or provided evidence.

V02.title: Meaning changed
V02.instructions: Does the candidate materially alter any claim, qualifier, causal relationship, commitment, or important implication of the original without authorization?

criteria.true: A material change to intended meaning appears in the revision.
criteria.false: Meaning is preserved or changed only where authorized by the instructions.

V03.title: Citation integrity broken
V03.instructions: Does the candidate remove, misattach, or change a citation or quoted passage such that an important assertion no longer has its original source context?

criteria.true: A reference, quote, or source-to-claim relationship is lost or distorted.
criteria.false: Source pointers and the claims they justify retain their intended relationships.

V04.title: Distinctive voice erased
V04.instructions: Does the candidate flatten deliberate humor, idiom, sentence rhythm, technical voice, stance, or personality that the author intended to keep?

criteria.true: A distinctive intentional feature is replaced by generic neutral copy without reader benefit.
criteria.false: The revision retains author choices unless they are specifically approved for editing.

V05.title: Reader-value comparison
V05.instructions: Compared with `original.text`, which statement best describes `candidate.text` for the specified reader and purpose?

criteria.better: The revision is more useful or more pleasurable to read, without losing important substance or voice.
criteria.equivalent: Changes are mainly stylistic; a reader receives about the same value and clarity.
criteria.worse: The revision loses useful meaning, precision, voice, or ease of reading.
criteria.unclear: The difference is too ambiguous to judge reliably from the supplied state.

V06.title: Substantive defect remains
V06.instructions: Does the revision leave the specific verified issue in `finding` substantially unresolved, even if its surface phrasing has changed?

criteria.true: The targeted relevance, reasoning, specificity, or structure failure remains.
criteria.false: The specific issue is resolved, or was already shown to be a false positive.
